title: The AI Toy Chest — prompts and demos
event: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 · 6:00–8:30 PM · Hudson Grille Midtown, upstairs
intro: Tonight’s focus: ChatGPT dots and Meta Muse as personal assistants, then Google Stitch for a playful game prototype. Pick one project or follow along with a partner. Drew’s Android X-Wing/REA story is an optional bonus if time permits.

challenges.title: 01 / ChatGPT dots — your event scout
challenges.prompt: Every Monday at 9:00 AM America/New_York, for the next four weeks, research upcoming Atlanta technology and AI events in the following seven days. My interests are hands-on AI tools, beginner-friendly learning, and meeting local builders. Find three worth considering. For each, include its date, local time, venue, registration link, cost or eligibility restrictions, and one sentence on why it fits. Use organizer pages and link your sources. If you cannot verify three, return fewer and explain the gap. Prepare a concise briefing and ask before adding anything to my calendar, registering, paying, or contacting anyone. Confirm the schedule and end date; if recurring work is unavailable, tell me and produce only this week's briefing.
challenges.result: A sourced shortlist with dates, venues, registration links, restrictions and reasons. Recurrence only if the product confirms it.
challenges.check: Open one organizer link. Check the date, venue and eligibility; inspect schedule confirmation.

steps: Sign in to ChatGPT in a desktop browser, desktop app, or the latest mobile app. Mobile web does not support dot setup.
Open dots, follow the introduction, and name your dot. App connections are optional for this public-event exercise.
Paste the prompt, review one source, then change an interest. Check the schedule confirmation before expecting recurring briefings.

challenges.title: 02 / Meta Muse — your weekend assistant
challenges.prompt: Help me plan an enjoyable Saturday afternoon in Atlanta for two adults. We have four hours and a maximum budget of $40 per person, excluding travel. We like vintage toys, casual food, and discovering something new. Ask one question if you need a preference before starting. Research two possible plans, including an indoor option. For each stop, link an official source and check opening hours, price, booking requirements, and travel assumptions; mark anything you cannot verify. Recommend one plan and explain the tradeoff. Draft the itinerary for me to review. Do not book, buy, send messages, connect accounts, or change my calendar. After you show the first version, I will say: It might rain and we only have two hours now. Revise the plan and explain what changed. If ongoing follow-up is supported, explain what you would need and ask before setting it up.
challenges.result: Two sourced options and a revised itinerary when your time and weather constraints change.
challenges.check: Open one official source. Check that the revised plan fits two hours and does not silently invent prices or travel times.

challenges.title: 03 / Google Stitch — Toy Chest Match
challenges.prompt: Design a playful, mobile-friendly memory matching game called Toy Chest Match, inspired by a 1980s arcade. Use six pairs of generic toy symbols: rocket, robot, alien, planet, joystick, and lightning bolt. Create a start screen, a board with twelve face-down cards, an attempts counter, a matches counter, and a win screen with Play Again. Make the cards large enough to tap and readable on a phone. Connect the screens into a clickable prototype. Show a correct match, a mismatch, and a completed game. Then change the theme from space toys to dinosaurs and add an easier three-pair mode. Explain which interactions are simulated and which actually run. Do not present mock counters or linked screens as a fully implemented matching engine. If running game logic needs another tool or an export step, tell me what remains.
challenges.result: A game design and clickable flow with start, play, and win states; identify any game logic still to implement.
challenges.check: Try a match, a mismatch, and Play Again. Does the prototype behave, or is it demonstrating a linked-screen simulation?

extras.title: 02 / Difficult Email Diplomat
extras.tool: Claude Skills, Codex Skills or Gemini Skills; follow the product’s own creation flow
extras.prompt: Create a reusable skill called Difficult Email Diplomat. Turn an awkward workplace or customer situation into a calm, firm email of at most 120 words. Ask one focused question if facts needed for the boundary are missing. State the situation without blame, preserve my boundary, and suggest a next step supported by my facts. Return a subject, draft, and a one-sentence check explaining which boundary you preserved. Never invent names, policies, concessions, deadlines, availability, or promises. Draft only; do not send. Save it as a skill using this product's supported method and tell me how to reuse it. First test: My coworker keeps scheduling meetings during my lunch break. Ask them to check my availability and choose a time outside lunch. Use a generic greeting. Then use the same skill for this new situation: A customer wants a full redesign by tomorrow, outside the agreed scope. I cannot commit to that deadline. Ask for their priorities so I can propose a revised scope and timeline. Do not promise a date or free work.
extras.result: One reusable instruction set and two short emails for different situations.
extras.check: Both drafts keep the requested boundary and avoid invented policies, dates, names or promises.

extras.title: 04 / Quantum, explained
extras.tool: Gemini Notebook or Gemini study notebooks, depending on account access
extras.prompt: Use only these two sources: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/qubit and https://www.nist.gov/quantum-information-science/quantum-computing-explained . Teach a curious 14-year-old the difference between a bit, a qubit, superposition, and measurement. Start with a short illustrated explanation and state the limits of any analogy. Then create a three-question interactive quiz with feedback after each answer. Include one question about why measurement does not reveal every possible answer at once. Cite the source section for every explanation and answer. If a source cannot be read, tell me instead of filling gaps. Finish by asking which idea I want to explore next.
extras.result: A short source-based explanation and a three-question interactive quiz with cited feedback.
extras.check: Answer incorrectly, inspect feedback, and open its supporting source passage.

extras.title: 06 / Build your weekend picker
extras.tool: Codex in a working local environment
extras.prompt: Build a working local weekend-idea app with interests, maximum budget, and available-time filters. Include sample activities with descriptions, illustrative costs per person, and durations. Label them as examples, not live venue listings. Save favorite ideas in browser storage. extras.title: Advanced bonus / Claude Code mod
extras.prompt: Create a Claude Code mod that adds a small pane beside the conversation showing the number of completed tool calls in this session. Start at zero. Increment once per completed tool call, including failed calls, and keep the count visible while I keep working. Use the type declarations and supported mod API from my installed Claude Code version; look up every event and UI method instead of guessing. Do not change permission decisions, rewrite prompts, log file contents, or make network requests. Show me the generated files and explain how to disable the mod. Demonstrate the display before and after reading two harmless sample files.
extras.result: Proposed tool-call count pane. Not built or rehearsed in Claude Code during preparation.
